question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is shadow. It derives from OE sceadu (with an already short /æ/ that became /æ/~/a/ in ModE), and unlike the others—where we see clear alternations from long vowels in disyllabic bases to lax vowels under trisyllabic conditions (south ~ southern, derive ~ derivative, serene ~ serenity, please ~ pleasant, grate ~ gratitude)—shadow shows no evidence of ever having participated in that lengthening-then-laxing cycle; its vowel quality has been consistently short since Old English.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow. Trisyllabic laxing applies in words like southern (south + -ern yielding the short vowel), derivative (from derive), serenity (from serene), gratitude (from grateful/grace), and pleasant (from please), where a historically long vowel shortens before two following syllables. Shadow, by contrast, descends from Old English sceadu (already disyllabic with a short vowel nucleus) and never had the trisyllabic environment that would trigger the change, so its vowel quality stayed stable through later developments.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is shadow, as it derives from Old English sceadu (with a short vowel nucleus already present in early forms like sceadwe), showing no evidence of a prior long vowel that would have been eligible for later trisyllabic laxing in Middle English. By contrast, southern shows the expected shortening from sūth, derivative from derive, serenity from serene, gratitude from grateful, and pleasant from please—all of which display the classic long-to-lax shift when a third syllable is added. Shadow simply never participated in that alternation to begin with.

Trisyllabic laxing is the regular English shortening/laxing of a tense/Latinate
vowel in a polysyllabic, normally Latinate, loan in which the stressed
syllable is followed by at least two more syllables.  In practice the
environment is a ≥3-syllable Latinate word with antepenultimate or
penultimate stress, e.g.

* serene /səˈriːn/  >  seren-ity /səˈrɛnəti/
* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > deriv-ative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* grate /ɡreɪt/    > grat-itude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/

The three Latinate loans in the set are exactly the ones that show the
classic trisyllabic environment:

* derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/, 4 syllables,
* serenity /səˈrɛnɪti/, 4 syllables, the /iː/ of serene is laxed to /ɛ/ in
the trisyllabic derivative,
* gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/, 3 syllables, the /eɪ/ of grate/grateful is
laxed to /æ/ in the trisyllabic form.

southern /ˈsʌðən/, pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ and, above all, shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/
are disyllabic Germanic items.  Shadow is a native Old English *sceadu
item and never has the ≥3-syllable Latinate environment on which
trisyllabic laxing operates, and it shows no Latinate vowel shortening
at all.  Southern and pleasant are for the same formal reason
disyllabic/Germanic/Romance disyllabic and do not enter the
trisyllabic laxing environment; the only clear non-Latinate,
non-trisyllabic member of the list is shadow.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

The five Latinate items all show the classic trisyllabic shortening / laxing that English does with a stressed long vowel when two or more post-tonic syllables are added by suffixation.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > deriv-ative /dɪˈrɪvəˌtɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > seren-ity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/ ~ /ɪ/
* pleas- /pliːz/ > pleas-ant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grat- /ɡreɪt/ > grat-itude /ˈɡrætiˌtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/ ~ /ʌ/ in the stressed base
* south /saʊθ/ > south-ern /ˈsʌðən/ ~ /ˈsaʊðən/  the long diphthongal base is laxed/reduced in the trisyllabic formation

shadow is a native Germanic formation, OE sceadu < *skadwa. The /eɪ/ ~ /æ/ alternation shade /ʃeɪd/ : shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is the regular Old English i-mutation / a-ablaut of the scead- root and not a case of trisyllabic shortening of a stressed long vowel on addition of a post-tonic syllable. It therefore has not undergone the trisyllabic laxing/shortening process shown by the other items.

The stem south /saʊθ/ retains the diphthong /aʊ/ in the compound and the word has never had the stressed-plus-two-unstressed syllable shape that conditions trisyllabic laxing. It is therefore the member of the set that is not a product of trisyllabic laxing, the two-syllable shadow/pleasant forms being the other non-trisyllabic items in the list.
